text_content: # Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet
normalized_text: # Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet

text_content: ## Introduction
normalized_text: ## Introduction

text_content: This article is focused on providing clear, simple, actionable guidance for preventing injection flaws in your applications. Injection attacks, for example [SQL Injection](https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/SQL_Injection), are unfortunately very common.
normalized_text: This article is focused on providing clear, simple, actionable guidance for preventing injection flaws in your applications. Injection attacks, for example [SQL Injection](https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/SQL_Injection), are unfortunately very common.

text_content: Application accessibility is a very important factor in protection and prevention of injection flaws. Only the minority of all applications within a company/enterprise are developed in house, where as most applications are from external sources. Open source applications give at least the opportunity to fix problems, but closed source applications need a different approach to injection flaws.
normalized_text: Application accessibility is a very important factor in protection and prevention of injection flaws. Only the minority of all applications within a company/enterprise are developed in house, where as most applications are from external sources. Open source applications give at least the opportunity to fix problems, but closed source applications need a different approach to injection flaws.

text_content: Injection flaws occur when an application sends untrusted data to an interpreter. Injection flaws are very prevalent, particularly in legacy code, often found in SQL queries, LDAP queries, XPath queries, OS commands, program arguments, etc. Injection flaws are easy to discover when examining code, but more difficult via testing. Scanners and fuzzers can help attackers find them.

Injection flaws are very prevalent, particularly in legacy code, often found in SQL queries, LDAP queries, XPath queries, OS commands, program arguments, etc. Injection flaws are easy to discover when examining code, but more difficult via testing. Scanners and fuzzers can help attackers find them.

text_content: Depending on the accessibility different actions must be taken in order to fix them. It is always the best way to fix the problem in source code itself, or even redesign some parts of the applications. But if the source code is not available or it is simply uneconomical to fix legacy software only virtual patching makes sense.

text_content: ## Application Types

text_content: Three classes of applications can usually be seen within a company. Those 3 types are needed to identify the actions which need to take place in order to prevent/fix injection flaws.

text_content: ### A1: New Application
normalized_text: ### A1: New Application

text_content: A new web application in the design phase, or in early stage development.

text_content: ### A2: Productive Open Source Application
normalized_text: ### A2: Productive Open Source Application

text_content: An already productive application, which can be easily adapted. A Model-View-Controller (MVC) type application is just one example of having a easily accessible application architecture.

text_content: #### LDAP Injection
normalized_text: #### LDAP Injection

text_content: LDAP Injection is an attack used to exploit web based applications that construct LDAP statements based on user input. When an application fails to properly sanitize user input, it's possible to modify LDAP statements through techniques similar to [SQL Injection](https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/SQL_Injection). LDAP injection attacks could result in the granting of permissions to unauthorized queries, and content modification inside the LDAP tree. For more information on LDAP Injection attacks, visit [LDAP injection](https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/LDAP_Injection).
normalized_text: LDAP Injection is an attack used to exploit web based applications that construct LDAP statements based on user input. When an application fails to properly sanitize user input, it's possible to modify LDAP statements through techniques similar to [SQL Injection](https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/SQL_Injection). LDAP injection attacks could result in the granting of permissions to unauthorized queries, and content modification inside the LDAP tree. For more information on LDAP Injection attacks, visit [LDAP injection](https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/LDAP_Injection).

text_content: [LDAP injection](https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/LDAP_Injection) attacks are common due to two factors:
normalized_text: [LDAP injection](https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/LDAP_Injection) attacks are common due to two factors:

text_content:
1. The lack of safer, parameterized LDAP query interfaces
2. The widespread use of LDAP to authenticate users to systems.

1. The lack of safer, parameterized LDAP query interfaces
2. The widespread use of LDAP to authenticate users to systems.

text_content: ##### Remediation
normalized_text: ##### Remediation

text_content: ###### Use the right LDAP encoding function
heading_path: Use the right LDAP encoding function
normalized_text: ###### Use the right LDAP encoding function

text_content: LDAP distinguished names and LDAP search filters require different escaping rules, defined by [RFC 4514](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4514) and [RFC 4515](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4515), respectively. Avoid custom escaping code and use a library encoder for the correct context. See the [LDAP Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet](LDAP_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.md) for current defenses and examples.

Avoid custom escaping code and use a library encoder for the correct context. text_content: ### Scripting languages
normalized_text: ### Scripting languages

text_content: All scripting languages used in web applications have a form of an `eval` call which receives code at runtime and executes it. If code is crafted using unvalidated and unescaped user input code injection can occur which allows an attacker to subvert application logic and eventually to gain local access.
normalized_text: All scripting languages used in web applications have a form of an `eval` call which receives code at runtime and executes it. If code is crafted using unvalidated and unescaped user input code injection can occur which allows an attacker to subvert application logic and eventually to gain local access.

text_content: Every time a scripting language is used, the actual implementation of the 'higher' scripting language is done using a 'lower' language like C. If the scripting language has a flaw in the data handling code '[Null Byte Injection](http://projects.webappsec.org/w/page/13246949/Null%20Byte%20Injection)' attack vectors can be deployed to gain access to other areas in memory, which results in a successful attack.

If the scripting language has a flaw in the data handling code '[Null Byte Injection](http://projects.webappsec.org/w/page/13246949/Null%20Byte%20Injection)' attack vectors can be deployed to gain access to other areas in memory, which results in a successful attack.

text_content: ### Operating System Commands
normalized_text: ### Operating System Commands

text_content: OS command injection is a technique used via a web interface in order to execute OS commands on a web server. The user supplies operating system commands through a web interface in order to execute OS commands.
normalized_text: OS command injection is a technique used via a web interface in order to execute OS commands on a web server. The user supplies operating system commands through a web interface in order to execute OS commands.

text_content: Any web interface that is not properly sanitized is subject to this exploit. With the ability to execute OS commands, the user can upload malicious programs or even obtain passwords. OS command injection is preventable when security is emphasized during the design and development of applications.
normalized_text: Any web interface that is not properly sanitized is subject to this exploit. With the ability to execute OS commands, the user can upload malicious programs or even obtain passwords. OS command injection is preventable when security is emphasized during the design and development of applications.

text_content: Check if any command execute methods are called and in unvalidated user input are taken as data for that command.
heading_path: How to test for the issue

text_content: Out side of that, appending a semicolon to the end of a URL query parameter followed by an operating system command, will execute the command. `%3B` is URL encoded and decodes to semicolon. This is because the `;` is interpreted as a command separator.

text_content: Example: `http://sensitive/something.php?dir=%3Bcat%20/etc/passwd`

text_content: If the application responds with the output of the `/etc/passwd` file then you know the attack has been successful. Many web application scanners can be used to test for this attack as they inject variations of command injections and test the response.

text_content: #### Remediation
normalized_text: #### Remediation

text_content: If it is considered unavoidable the call to a system command incorporated with user-supplied, the following two layers of defense should be used within software in order to prevent attacks
normalized_text: If it is considered unavoidable the call to a system command incorporated with user-supplied, the following two layers of defense should be used within software in order to prevent attacks

text_content:
1. **Parameterization** - If available, use structured mechanisms that automatically enforce the separation between data and command. These mechanisms can help to provide the relevant quoting, encoding.
2. **Input validation** - the values for commands and the relevant arguments should be both validated. There are different degrees of validation for the actual command and its arguments:
    - When it comes to the **commands** used, these must be validated against a list of allowed commands.
    - In regards to the **arguments** used for these commands, they should be validated using the following options:
        - Positive or allowlist input validation - where are the arguments allowed explicitly defined
        - Allow-list Regular Expression - where is explicitly defined a list of good characters allowed and the maximum length of the string. Ensure that metacharacters like `& | ; $ > < \` \ !` and whitespaces are not part of the Regular Expression. For example, the following regular expression only allows lowercase letters and numbers, and does not contain metacharacters. The length is also being limited to 3-10 characters:

text_content: ### Network Protocols
normalized_text: ### Network Protocols

text_content: Web applications often communicate with network daemons (like SMTP, IMAP, FTP) where user input becomes part of the communication stream. Here it is possible to inject command sequences to abuse an established session.

text_content: ## Injection Prevention Rules
normalized_text: ## Injection Prevention Rules

text_content: ### Rule \#1 (Perform proper input validation)
normalized_text: ### Rule \#1 (Perform proper input validation)

text_content: Perform proper input validation. Positive or allowlist input validation with appropriate canonicalization is also recommended, but **is not a complete defense** as many applications require special characters in their input.
normalized_text: Perform proper input validation. Positive or allowlist input validation with appropriate canonicalization is also recommended, but **is not a complete defense** as many applications require special characters in their input.

text_content: ### Rule \#2 (Use a safe API)
normalized_text: ### Rule \#2 (Use a safe API)

text_content: The preferred option is to use a safe API which avoids the use of the interpreter entirely or provides a parameterized interface. Be careful of APIs, such as stored procedures, that are parameterized, but can still introduce injection under the hood.
normalized_text: The preferred option is to use a safe API which avoids the use of the interpreter entirely or provides a parameterized interface. Be careful of APIs, such as stored procedures, that are parameterized, but can still introduce injection under the hood.

text_content: ### Rule \#3 (Contextually escape user data)
normalized_text: ### Rule \#3 (Contextually escape user data)

text_content: If a parameterized API is not available, you should carefully escape special characters using the specific escape syntax for that interpreter.
normalized_text: If a parameterized API is not available, you should carefully escape special characters using the specific escape syntax for that interpreter.
